newsitem.title: UK: London to stay top finance centre in or out of EMU - BOE.
newsitem.headline: London to stay top finance centre in or out of EMU - BOE.

text.p: London should remain Europe's main financial centre whether or not Britain joins European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), a Bank of England official said on Thursday.

"In many respects the euro, if sterling remains outside, would be just another foreign currency -- and London has operated extremely effectively in other people's currencies for years," Stephen Collins told a conference on EMU.

Collins, head of division in the BOE's monetary stability wing, said less than 10 percent of London's foreign exchange business was between currencies expected to join the first wave of EMU, much less than was the case for Frankfurt or Paris.
This meant the euro's creation would have proportionately much less effect on London than on Paris or Frankfurt.

"We are not complacent, and there is much to be done, but there are good grounds to be confident that the City (of London) will remain the pre-eminent financial centre of Europe, whether we are in or out of EMU," Collins said.

"If the euro is successfully shepherded into existence, it should result in an expansion of financial activity that can benefit all the main financial centres in Europe, inside or outside the euro area."
He said EMU should not call into question London's global role as one of the world's three major international centres alongside New York and Tokyo.
Nor should it undermine the advantages London enjoyed in its skilled workforce, technical infrastructure, regulatory framework, international language and critical mass of business.
Collins also brushed off fears London would suffer severely if denied access to the TARGET cross-border settlement system for the euro.
Banks in Germany and France have campaigned against equal credit treatment in the TARGET system for EMU "ins" and "outs".

Collins said London's foreign exchange market managed to have a huge proportion of world-wide global trading in the dollar and mark without any direct facility to make and settle payments in either the United States or Germany.

At the same time, he said everyone had a common interest in eliminating payment risk, nationally and internationally, "because the risks of systemic contagion through the payment mechanism are not constrained within national boundaries".
Collins said that if Britain stayed out of EMU, it would be vital to continue to pursue sound macro-economic policies, including monetary policy directed to price stability.
"That would both serve to allay suspicion in the euro area that we might seek unwarranted competitive advantage through the exchange rate, and would of course make sense in its own right."
